questions.question: Define a pathogen and a vector. Copy and complete for TB, cholera, HIV and malaria: pathogen, group of micro-organism, route of transmission.
questions.expected_answer: A pathogen is a micro-organism that causes disease. A vector is an animal, usually an insect, that carries a pathogen from one host to another. TB: TB bacterium, bacterium, airborne droplets from coughs and sneezes. Cholera: cholera bacterium, bacterium, water and food contaminated with faeces. HIV/AIDS: human immunodeficiency virus, virus, blood, semen, vaginal fluid and breast milk (unprotected sex, shared needles, mother to child). Malaria: Plasmodium, protist, bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito (vector).

questions.question: Explain the difference between HIV and AIDS, list three ways HIV is spread and three ways it is not spread, and explain how antiretroviral therapy helps.
questions.expected_answer: HIV is the virus; it attacks white blood cells that organise the immune system. AIDS is the late stage of untreated HIV infection, when the immune system is so weakened that the body cannot fight infections such as TB and pneumonia. Spread by: unprotected sex, sharing needles or contact with infected blood, mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. Not spread by: hugging, shaking hands, sharing cups, plates or toilets, coughing, swimming, mosquito bites. Antiretroviral therapy is a daily combination of medicines that stops the virus multiplying; taken consistently it keeps the virus undetectable, protects the immune system so the person lives a long healthy life, and prevents sexual transmission. There is no cure.

questions.question: For cholera and malaria, describe the main symptoms, the treatment and two methods of prevention, explaining which link in the chain of transmission each prevention method breaks.
questions.expected_answer: Cholera: sudden severe watery diarrhoea, vomiting, leg cramps, rapid dehydration. Treatment: oral rehydration solution (1 litre clean boiled cooled water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, half a level teaspoon salt), drip fluids in severe cases, sometimes antibiotics. Prevention: boiling or treating water kills the bacteria in the water route; proper sanitation keeps faeces out of drinking water; handwashing with soap removes bacteria before they reach food. Malaria: fever, chills, sweating, headache and body aches in waves, beginning about 1 to 4 weeks after the bite; severe cases cause anaemia, brain damage, death. Treatment: antimalarial drugs after a blood test. Prevention: insecticide-treated nets and repellent stop the vector biting; indoor spraying kills mosquitoes; removing standing water removes breeding sites; preventive tablets for travellers protect the host.
